body: — Riverbank Leisure Centre, good morning. Erin speaking.
— Oh, hello. I'd like to ask about joining, please. I've just moved into the area.
— Of course. I'll take a few details and then talk you through what we offer. Can I start with your surname?
— It's Whitfield.
— Could you spell that for me?
— Yes — W, H, I, T, F, I, E, L, D. Whitfield.
— Thank you. And a contact number?
— It's oh-seven-double-four, one-nine-six, three-eight-two. Sorry, that's my old one. Let me give you the new one — oh-seven-double-four, one-nine-six, three-two-eight.

— Three-two-eight at the end. Got it. Now, we run three kinds of membership. There's Standard, which is the gym and the pool. There's Active, which adds every class on the timetable. And there's Family, which covers two adults and up to three children.
— It would just be me. But I'd want the classes — I'm trying to get back into swimming properly, and there's a technique session I saw on your website.
— Then Active is the one you want. Standard wouldn't include that session.
— Active, then.
— Lovely. Active is normally fifty-two pounds a month. There's an introductory rate for the first three months, though, which brings it down to forty-five.
— Forty-five. That's better than I expected.

— It goes up to the full fifty-two in month four, so do bear that in mind. Now, everyone joining does a short induction before their first visit — it's about forty minutes with one of the instructors.
— When are those?
— We run them Tuesdays and Thursdays. This week Tuesday's already full, I'm afraid, so the next one would be Thursday.
— Thursday's fine.
— And the times are ten in the morning or six in the evening.
— Six, please. I don't finish work until half past four.
— Six it is. Do come in something you can move in — you'll be shown the machines and you'll actually use a couple of them. And bring a towel; we don't provide those.
— A towel. Right.
— One more thing about the lockers. They take a one-pound coin, and you get it back when you return the key — but if you lose the key there's a charge of fifteen pounds for a replacement.
— Fifteen. I'll be careful with it.
— Most people are. Now, was there a particular class you wanted me to book you onto? The technique one you mentioned is called Stroke Clinic, and it fills up.
— Yes, please — Stroke Clinic.
— Stroke Clinic, Thursday evenings after your induction. And last thing, for our records: how did you hear about the centre?
— A colleague, actually. Someone at work swims here.
— A recommendation. That's what most people say. Right, Mr Whitfield, you're all set. See you Thursday at six.

body: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for giving up your Saturday. Before we put anyone to work, let me walk you round the plan so you know where things are — you'll be surprised how often people end up watering the wrong beds.

So. You've come in through the gate at the bottom left, and the main path runs straight up from there, then turns right along the middle of the site. Keep that shape in your head and you won't get lost.
The site is two rows of plots. The top row runs along the river; the bottom row is the one you walk past on your way in from the gate.

So, first, the tool store. That's on the bottom row, the very first plot you come to from the entrance. Everything is signed inside and there's a list on the door — please put things back where the list says, not where there's a gap.

The compost area is on the same bottom row, but right along at the other end. Not the last plot — the one before it, third along. People do get this wrong, so: third along the bottom, with the pond after it.
Up on the top row now, along the river. The fruit cages are the first plot up there, directly above the tool store. They're netted, so the door is stiff — lift it rather than pull it.

The polytunnel is the biggest structure we have. It's on the top row too, at the far end, the very last plot in that row. It gets the afternoon sun in that corner, which is the whole reason it went there rather than nearer the gate.

And finally the wildlife pond, which is the one I want everyone to be careful around. It is the very last plot on the bottom row, in the corner. There's no fence — that's deliberate, for the hedgehogs — so watch your step, particularly if you've brought children.
Right. A few practical things.

First, the question everyone asks: can you take produce home? Yes, but not on your first day, and not by the bagful. The rule is that anything harvested on a session day goes to the share table by the entrance, and whatever's left at four o'clock, volunteers may take. It isn't about trust; it's that a share table is how we keep the neighbours on our side.

Second, tools. The powered tools — the mower and the strimmer — are for trained volunteers only, and the training runs once a month. Hand tools, anyone can use. Please don't be the person who decides today is the day they learn to strim.

Third, wet weather. We do not cancel for rain. We cancel for high wind, because of the trees along the river, and you'll get a text by eight in the morning if a session is off. If you haven't had a text, assume we're on.

Fourth, and this one has caught people out: parking. The car park behind the centre is not ours. It belongs to the health centre and they do issue tickets at weekends. There's free parking on Mill Lane, two minutes' walk, and that is what we'd recommend.

And last of all — what we most need from new volunteers is not muscle, honestly. It's people who come back. One person here every other Saturday for a year is worth far more to this garden than twenty people once.

narratorIntro: Now turn to Part two. You will hear a librarian briefing a group of new volunteers. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to twenty.

body: Good morning, and thank you for coming in early. I want to walk you through the building before it opens, because most of what goes wrong on a first shift is somebody sending a reader to the wrong floor with complete confidence.

We are on four levels and they are not numbered the way you would expect. The ground floor is what we call the Street floor, because it has the door on it. Below that is the Lower floor, which is not a basement and does have windows. Above the Street floor are the First and the Second.
So. Newspapers and the current magazines are on the Lower floor, at the back, past the lift. People assume they are near the door because they are quick to read, and they are not.
The children's library has the whole of the First floor. It has its own toilets and its own entrance from the car park, which matters on a wet Tuesday when a class arrives.

Local history is on the Second floor, and it is the only collection that does not lend. Everything there is consulted at the desk and stays in the room. If somebody asks to borrow a parish register, the answer is no, and the reason is that there is one of it.

The photocopier is on the Street floor beside the returns machine, and the study rooms are on the Second, along the corridor from local history. Do not send anyone to the First floor for a study room; the rooms up there are for staff and one of them is where we eat lunch.
Now, some practical things, and I would rather over-explain than have you guess.

Fines. We do not charge them any more, on children's books or adult books. What we do charge for is a lost item, and the charge is the replacement cost, not a fixed fee. If a reader tells you they have been fined, they are remembering an old system.

Second: the self-service machines take a card but they will not renew an item that somebody else has reserved. The machine says so in very small type, so the reader will come to you convinced it is broken. It is not.

Third, and this is the one I want you to remember: you may not look up what a reader has borrowed and tell somebody else, including their husband, their wife, or a police officer without a warrant. If you are asked, the answer is that you cannot, and you may send them to me. Nobody will be cross with you for saying no.
Fourth, the volunteer shift is three hours, and we ask you to take fifteen minutes of it as a break, in the staff room and not at the desk. People skip it and then get short with somebody at the end.

And finally, what we actually need. It is not shelving, honestly, although there is always shelving. It is somebody willing to walk a reader to the shelf rather than pointing. That one habit changes what people think of this building more than anything else we do.

body: Welcome, all of you. I am going to speak for about ten minutes and then you can go and unpack. Most of this is on the sheet in your room, but people do not read the sheet, so here it is out loud.

The site is five blocks around a courtyard. They are named after rivers. That sounded charming to somebody in nineteen-sixty. It is now simply five names you have to learn: Avon, Brent, Colne, Derwent and Erne.

The laundry is in Brent, on the ground floor. It is the only one. Please do not carry a basket around all five blocks looking for another. The bicycle store is in Erne, at the far end from the gate. It opens with the same card as your room.

The post arrives at the porters' desk in Avon. That is the block with the arch. Sorting is into pigeonholes by surname and not by block. Parcels are held there too. The kitchen for anyone in a studio without one is in Colne. It is shared with the common room. Consequently it is noisy in the evening and deserted in the morning.
Quiet hours run from eleven at night to seven in the morning, every night, including Saturday. I will be honest that Friday is enforced less strictly than Tuesday, but do not rely on that.

On kitchens: each floor has one and each floor cleans it. We do not have a cleaner for kitchens, and the reason is not money. It is that a cleaner meant nobody ever spoke to anybody about the state of it, and the kitchens were worse.

Maintenance goes through the portal, not to me, and not to the porters. A message to me has to be typed into the portal by somebody. That somebody is me at eleven at night. If it is a leak or a smell of gas, then find a person immediately and do not use the portal at all.
Guests may stay two nights in any week. You must sign them in at the porters' desk. The reason is fire, not suspicion. If the building empties at three in the morning we count heads against a list.
The deposit is two hundred pounds. It comes back in full unless something is broken. Ordinary marks on a wall are not something broken. A hole in a door is.
One last thing. The first fortnight is the loudest and the least representative. If you decide in week one that you have made a mistake, wait until week three before you decide it again.

narratorIntro: Now turn to Part two. You will hear a ranger briefing new guides at a wildlife reserve. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to twenty.
narratorOutro: That is the end of Part two.
body: Good morning. You have all walked the reserve once as visitors. Today I want you to learn it as guides. That is a different thing. A guide has to know where not to take people.

The reserve divides into five zones and we use the same five names on every map and every radio call. The Reedbed is the wet ground at the eastern end. The Scrape is the shallow water with the islands in it. The Carr is the wet woodland. The Heath is the dry open ground on the ridge. And the Meadow is the field by the car park, which most visitors think is the whole reserve.
The main hide, the one with the ramp, looks over the Scrape. That is where you take anyone who cannot walk far. It is also where the birds are. Nobody is being handed the consolation option.

The pond dipping platform is in the Meadow, deliberately, because it is loud and children fall in. The nesting terns are on the Scrape as well. They sit on the far islands. That is why the telescope in the hide matters.
The boardwalk runs through the Carr. It is closed from the first of the month for repairs. If a visitor asks, do not say it is closed because of nesting; that is next spring and this is carpentry.
Adders are on the Heath. They are there every year and they are not aggressive. The reason we mention them is not danger but dogs. Dogs stay on the lead on the ridge.
Now, three things about guiding rather than about the reserve.

First, do not promise a species. Say to a family that they will see a kingfisher and you have made the next ninety minutes a disappointment. Say what has been seen this week. That information is on the board by the door, updated every morning.

Second, the reserve is quiet in the middle of the day and there is nothing wrong with saying so. A guide who fills a silent hour with continuous talking has taught people that nothing was happening. A guide who says the birds are resting has taught them something true.

Third, and this is the one guides get wrong for years: your group will look where you look. Point with your whole arm at nothing and twenty people will examine that nothing for a minute. They will trust you slightly less afterwards.

And if you are asked a question you cannot answer, say so and write it on the board. Somebody who works here will know, and the visitor will remember the answer arriving more than they would have remembered you having it.

— Good. Section three, the cycling case study — that's Amsterdam and Copenhagen.

— Perfect, it's yours. Section four is the bus network modelling, and that's the one I'm nervous about, because it needs the software.

— Which is why I'd rather one of us learns it well than both of us learn it badly. I'll take it. I've got a fortnight before it's due and I'd rather that be my problem.

— That's a fair point. Both, then.
— And section six, the cost comparison.
— I'll do that one too. It's spreadsheets, and I'm faster at spreadsheets than you are.
— I'm not going to pretend otherwise.
— Right. Now — the part I actually wanted to talk about. Doctor Ellis said our research question was too broad.
— She did. Although what she actually said was that it was too broad for the time we have. That's not the same as it being a bad question.
— No, it isn't. So do we narrow it, or do we keep it and say clearly what we couldn't cover?
— I'd narrow it. A report that admits it couldn't cover half its own question reads as though we ran out of time — which we did, but we don't have to advertise it.
— See, I'd go the other way. I think naming the limits is what makes it look deliberate rather than rushed.

— Now, the presentation. Twenty minutes for six sections is three minutes each, which is nothing.
— We don't present all six. We present the two case studies properly and summarise the rest in one slide.
— Doctor Ellis will ask about the modelling, though. She always asks about the method.
— Then we have a slide ready for it, but we don't lead with it. There's a difference between being ready for a question and spending eight of our twenty minutes on it.

narratorIntro: Now turn to Part four. You will hear a lecturer talking about urban heat and how cities are responding to it. First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
narratorOutro: That is the end of Part four.
body: Good afternoon. Today I want to talk about a problem that is easy to measure, hard to see, and increasingly expensive: the fact that a city is warmer than the countryside around it. The phenomenon has a name — the urban heat island — and I want to cover three things. What causes it, what it costs, and what actually works.

Let's begin with the cause, because there is a common misunderstanding here. People assume the heat is produced by the city: by cars, by air conditioning, by industry. Some of it is, but that is the smaller part. The larger part is not produced at all. It is stored.

Concrete, brick and asphalt have a high thermal mass. They absorb solar radiation through the day and release it slowly through the night. A field cools quickly after sunset; a street does not. And so the difference between a city and its surroundings is at its greatest not at noon, as you might expect, but a few hours after dark. In a large European city that night-time difference typically reaches four degrees, and in extreme conditions it has been measured above seven.

The second contributor is the absence of water. In a landscape with vegetation, a large share of incoming energy goes into evaporating water from leaves and soil — a process called evapotranspiration — and energy spent evaporating water is energy not spent raising the temperature. Pave that landscape and the water runs off into a drain within minutes. The cooling mechanism has been removed, and nothing replaced it.

The third is geometry. Narrow streets between tall buildings behave like a series of traps: radiation bounces between the walls rather than escaping upwards. Researchers describe this using the sky view factor — essentially, how much of the sky you can see from street level. The less sky, the less heat escapes.
So much for the cause. Now the cost.

The obvious cost is health, and it falls unevenly. During the 2003 heatwave in western Europe, mortality rose most sharply among people over seventy-five living alone on upper floors of buildings without ventilation. Heat is not distributed evenly across a city, and neither is the ability to escape it. The neighbourhoods that are hottest are, with tedious reliability, the neighbourhoods with the least tree cover, and those are rarely the wealthy ones.

The less obvious cost is energy. Air conditioning is a feedback loop: it cools a building by moving heat outside, which warms the street, which raises the demand for air conditioning. In dense districts this can raise the outdoor temperature by a further degree overnight.
Which brings me to what works, and here I want to be careful, because this field has a weakness for the photogenic solution.

The most effective intervention, by a wide margin, is trees — mature trees, in streets, in enough numbers to form a continuous canopy. Shade prevents the surface from absorbing the heat in the first place, which is worth more than removing it afterwards, and the evapotranspiration adds cooling on top. Measurements of well-shaded streets consistently show surface temperatures around ten degrees below unshaded ones nearby.

Second: surface colour. Painting roofs white, or using reflective paving, raises what is called the albedo — the proportion of sunlight reflected rather than absorbed. It is cheap, it works, and it is unglamorous.

Third, and this is the one I would ask you to be sceptical about: green roofs. They are popular with planners and they photograph beautifully. They do cool the building beneath them, and they help with rainfall. But a green roof five storeys up does very little for the temperature of the street below, and the street is where people actually are. It is not that they do not work. It is that they are frequently used to answer a question they were never designed to address.

The pattern across all three is the same. The interventions that work best are the ones that stop heat being absorbed, rather than the ones that deal with it afterwards. Next week we will look at how these measures are costed, and why the cheapest of them is so often the last to be funded.

narratorIntro: Now turn to Part three. You will hear two students, Rachel and Tomás, deciding what to do about an experiment that did not work. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to thirty.
narratorOutro: That is the end of Part three.
body: — So. Run four is wrong and we both know it.
— I don't know that it's wrong. I know it doesn't match the other three.
— Which is what wrong means, Tomás.
— No, it is what anomalous means, and the difference matters here: wrong would mean that we made a mistake somewhere, and I have been through the log twice without finding one.
— The temperature drifted.

— It drifted by half a degree, which is comfortably inside the tolerance we wrote down before we started, so if half a degree is enough to move the result that far then the interesting finding is the half degree rather than the run.
— Or the probe was failing.
— That I'll grant you. The probe is nine years old and the calibration certificate expired in March.
— So we have two candidate explanations and no way to choose between them.
— We have one way. Repeat run four with the new probe.
— Which costs us a fortnight we don't have.
— Then here is the honest question. What do we write if we don't repeat it?
— We write that we observed an anomaly, we set out both explanations as fairly as we can, and we say plainly that we were not able to distinguish between them with the runs we had.
— And Doctor Ellis will ask why we didn't repeat it.
— And we answer that a repeat would have cost two weeks which we judged were better spent on the other four runs, which is a defensible position even though it is not a comfortable one to defend.
— I'd rather be uncomfortable and honest than comfortable and quiet. But I still want the repeat.
— Say why.
— Because if the probe is genuinely failing then runs one to three are suspect as well, and we have already written three-quarters of a report resting on them.
— That is a much better argument than the one you started with.
— I know. I got there while you were talking.
— All right. We repeat run four, and we do it with the borrowed probe from the second lab rather than waiting for ours to be calibrated.
— Can we borrow it?
— Marta says yes if we book it for a morning, because the second lab uses it in the afternoons and she is not willing to move that for us.
— A morning is enough for one run, provided we set the bath up the night before and leave it running so the temperature has settled by the time we get there.

— Then that's the plan. And whichever way it comes out, the anomaly goes in the report. If the repeat matches the others we say the first attempt was instrument error and we caught it. If it doesn't, we've found something.
— And if the repeat is different from both?
— Then we have a very short discussion with Doctor Ellis and a much longer chapter.

narratorIntro: Now turn to Part three. You will hear a student, Nadia, discussing a draft dissertation chapter with her supervisor. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to thirty.
narratorOutro: That is the end of Part three.
body: — Come in, Nadia. I've read the chapter twice, which is more than I usually manage, and I want to start with what is working.
— That would be a change.

— The literature section is genuinely good, because you have organised it by argument rather than by decade, which almost nobody manages at this stage, and the effect of doing it that way is that a reader can see immediately what is actually contested and what is merely repeated.
— That took the longest.
— It shows, and it was worth it. The methods section is where I want to spend our time.
— I thought it might be.
— You describe what you did very clearly. What you do not do is say why you did it that way rather than another way. At the moment a reader has to take the design on trust.
— I assumed that was obvious from the research question.

— It is obvious to you because you have lived with it for eight months, whereas an examiner who reads the whole thing in a single afternoon has no way of telling an unstated reason from an absent one, so an unjustified choice reads as a choice you did not know you were making.
— So I need a paragraph on why interviews rather than a survey.
— A paragraph, and one on why twelve interviews rather than thirty. Not an apology. A reason.

narratorIntro: Now turn to Part four. You will hear a lecturer talking about how the seabed is mapped. First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
narratorOutro: That is the end of Part four.
body: Good morning. I want to talk today about how we know the shape of the sea floor, which is a subject where the honest answer to almost every question is that we know far less than people assume, and where the reason we know anything at all is a single physical fact: sound travels through water very much better than light does.

Let me begin with the method that is still the foundation of everything. A ship carries a device called a transducer, which converts an electrical signal into a pulse of sound and then, a moment later, converts the returning echo back into electricity. The instrument measures the time between the two, and because the speed of sound in seawater is roughly fifteen hundred metres a second, half that time multiplied by that speed gives the depth beneath the hull.

That sentence contains the whole method and also the whole difficulty, because the speed is not in fact constant. It varies with temperature, with pressure and with salinity, and a survey that assumes a single value will produce a chart that is systematically wrong in a way no amount of care in the measuring can correct. Serious surveys therefore lower an instrument that records the sound speed at every depth before any mapping begins, and that profile, rather than the textbook number, is what the calculation uses.

The second development was to stop asking about one point at a time. A single-beam echo sounder measures the depth directly under the ship and nothing else, so a survey is a set of lines with unmeasured water between them, and the cartographer draws the gaps in. Multibeam systems send out a fan of beams across the track and measure a swathe of the floor at once, typically about four times the water depth in width. That is the reason deep water is cheaper to survey per square kilometre than shallow water, which surprises people until they see the geometry.

Now, the coverage. If you take the whole ocean floor and ask how much of it has been measured directly in this way, at a resolution useful for anything, the figure is about a quarter. The rest of what you see on a map of the sea floor is derived from satellite altimetry — the satellite measures the height of the sea surface very precisely, and because a seamount has mass, the water above it stands very slightly higher. That works, and the resolution is nothing like the same: a feature has to be several kilometres across before it disturbs the surface enough to be seen.

Which brings me to the practical consequence, and it is not a scientific one. Uncharted features are a hazard to shipping, and the ones that matter are exactly the ones the satellite method cannot resolve — a pinnacle two hundred metres across in otherwise deep water is invisible from orbit and perfectly capable of removing the bottom of a vessel.

And the last point, which I want you to be sceptical about when you read popular accounts. It is often said that we have better maps of Mars than of the ocean floor. As a statement about resolution that is broadly true. As a statement about difficulty it is misleading, because the reason is not that the problem is harder but that the ocean is opaque to the instruments that made those Martian maps, and the instrument that does work has to be dragged through the water at the speed of a ship.
Next week we will look at what the same technique tells us about the sediment beneath the floor, rather than the floor itself.

narratorIntro: Now turn to Part four. You will hear a lecturer talking about the shipping container. First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
narratorOutro: That is the end of Part four.
body: Good afternoon. I want to spend this hour on an object that is deliberately boring, because the interesting thing about the shipping container is that almost none of its importance is in the box itself.

The box was not a new idea. Wooden containers moved on railways in the nineteenth century, and several companies tried steel ones in the nineteen-twenties without anything much happening. What changed in the nineteen-fifties was not the container but the agreement about the container, and specifically an agreement on the corner fitting — the steel casting at each of the eight corners that lets a crane pick the box up, and lets one box lock to another. Once that casting was standardised, a container loaded in one country could be lifted by a crane built in another, and everything else followed from that.

So consider what the old system cost. Before containers, cargo moved as what was called break bulk: sacks, barrels, crates, each handled individually. A ship might spend as long in port as it spent at sea, and the labour of loading was a very large share of the total cost of moving anything. The figure usually quoted is that handling accounted for roughly half the cost of an ocean voyage, and the striking part is that this cost did not fall with distance. Doubling the length of a voyage barely changed it.

That last point is the one I want you to hold onto, because it explains the consequence. When handling collapses as a share of cost, distance becomes cheap in a way it had never been, and a factory can be sited according to wages and land rather than according to proximity to the customer. The container did not cause that pattern on its own — tariffs and communications matter too — but it removed the friction that had held it back.
Now, three things that are usually left out.

The first is that the ports which won were not the ports which had been winning. A container terminal needs deep water, a great deal of flat land behind the quay, and rail access. Old city docks, hemmed in by the city that had grown around them, had none of those, and the traffic moved to places that had been minor or did not exist. That is a redistribution rather than a growth, and the places that lost did not get it back.

The second is labour. The number of dockworkers required per ton fell by an enormous factor, and the disputes of the nineteen-sixties and seventies were not irrational resistance to progress; they were an accurate reading of what was about to happen to a trade.

The third is that the standard has a cost of its own. The corner fitting fixes the maximum dimensions, which fixes the geometry of the crane, the width of the ship and the height of the bridges under which the train will pass. Any improvement that would require a different box is now practically impossible, because the box is the least valuable part of a system built around it. Economists call this lock-in, and the container is the clearest example I know.
Next week: what happens to the standard when the cargo changes shape, and why refrigerated units break the pattern.

narratorIntro: Now turn to Part four. You will hear a lecturer talking about soil compaction on farms. First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
narratorOutro: That is the end of Part four.
body: Good morning. Today's subject is a problem that is invisible from the surface, expensive to fix, and largely created by the machinery that was bought to make the work easier. I mean the compaction of agricultural soil.

Let me start with what soil is, structurally, because the whole argument depends on it. A healthy agricultural soil is roughly half solid material and half pore space, and the pores matter more than the solids. They hold the water, they carry the air that roots need, and they provide the channels along which a root can travel without having to force its way. Compaction is simply the loss of that pore space under load, and it is a change in the arrangement of the soil rather than in its composition.

The load, of course, is the machine. And here is the fact that surprises people: the weight of farm machinery has increased by a factor of about ten since the nineteen-sixties, while the area of tyre in contact with the ground has not increased anything like as fast. The pressure at the surface is governed mainly by the inflation pressure of the tyre, which is why a wider tyre helps at the surface. But the stress deeper down is governed by the total axle load, and no tyre design changes that. So the modern machine has solved the shallow problem and made the deep one considerably worse.

That distinction between shallow and deep matters, because they are different problems with different prospects. Compaction in the top twenty-five centimetres can be lifted by cultivation, or by a winter of freezing and thawing, or by roots. Below about forty centimetres, none of those reach. Frost does not penetrate that far in most climates, the plough does not go there, and the roots that could break it are the roots that the compaction is preventing. Deep compaction is therefore effectively permanent on any timescale a farmer plans over.

The costs are of three kinds. Yield falls, and typical measured losses run between ten and twenty-five per cent on affected ground. Water does not infiltrate, so rainfall runs off the surface instead of entering the soil, which means both drought stress in the field and flooding downstream from it. And in waterlogged compacted soil, nitrogen is lost to the atmosphere as nitrous oxide, which is a greenhouse gas of considerable strength.

What works, then. The most effective single measure is not a machine at all: it is confining traffic to permanent lanes, so that the same narrow strips are driven over every year and the rest of the field is never touched. Trials consistently show the largest benefit of anything tested, and the objection is not that it fails but that it requires the machinery to match the lane spacing, which is a capital decision rather than an agronomic one.

And the measure I would ask you to be sceptical about is deep loosening — dragging a tine through the compacted layer to break it up. It works, it is expensive in fuel, and unless the traffic pattern that caused the compaction changes, the soil is back where it started within about three years. It treats the symptom on a field where the cause is still driving over it every spring.
Next week we will look at how compaction is actually measured, and why the penetrometer readings in most published studies are less comparable than they appear.

narratorIntro: Now turn to Part two. You will hear a woman welcoming new volunteers to a community garden. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to twenty.
body: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Fenwick Community Garden. I'm Priya, and I coordinate the volunteers here. I'll take about ten minutes to tell you how the garden runs, and then we'll walk round it together.

First, the practical things. We are open every day from eight in the morning until dusk, but volunteer sessions are on Tuesdays and Saturdays only. Tuesday sessions run from ten until one. Saturday sessions are longer, from nine until three, and lunch is provided on Saturdays but not on Tuesdays, so bring something with you if you come midweek.

You will have seen the sign-in book by the gate. Please use it every time. It is not for checking up on anyone; it is what our insurance requires, and if the book says nobody is here, then officially nobody is here.

Now, the tools. The shed is unlocked during sessions and the code is only given to session leaders, so please don't take tools home even overnight. Everything comes back to the shed clean. There is a brush and a bucket by the door for that. The one thing I ask you to be careful with is the rotavator, which is heavy and is used by trained volunteers only.

About the plots. The garden is divided into three areas. The beds nearest the gate are the community beds, and everything grown there is shared. The middle section is the orchard, which needs almost nothing from us except in autumn. The far end is the wildlife area, and that one is deliberately left rough. Please don't tidy it. Every year somebody weeds it with the best intentions, and every year we lose the frogs.

We do ask for one thing that surprises people. If you take vegetables home, write them in the produce book. We are not counting what anyone takes, and there is no limit. We report the total weight to the council, and that figure is what keeps our lease at a peppercorn rent.

Finally, the children's sessions. Those run in the school holidays, on Wednesday mornings, and we need two extra adults each time. If you'd like to help with those, speak to Marcus rather than to me. He organises them and I never know the dates until he tells me.

narratorIntro: Now turn to Part two. You will hear a man explaining the arrangements at a residents' car park. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to twenty.
body: Good evening. Thank you for coming. I'm the building manager, and I've called this meeting because the car park arrangements change on the first of next month, and I would rather explain them now than answer forty emails afterwards.

Here is what is changing and, just as importantly, what is not. The number of spaces is not changing. There are fifty-two, there have always been fifty-two, and nobody is losing a space. What changes is how they are allocated.

Until now, spaces have been numbered and each flat has had its own. That sounds fair and it has not worked, because about a third of the spaces stand empty on any given day while visitors circle the block. From the first, the parking becomes unnumbered. You park in any space that is free, and your permit is what entitles you to be there rather than a particular rectangle of tarmac.

Permits arrive by post next week. Each flat gets one as before. If you want a second, there is a waiting list, and I will be honest with you: it is nineteen names long and it moves about twice a year.

The eight spaces along the north wall are the exception. Four of those are accessible bays and stay reserved, and they are enforced. The other four become visitor spaces, bookable through the building app for up to four hours. You book them under your own flat number, so if a visitor overstays it is your permit that gets the notice.

Charging points. There are two, and they are staying where they are, but the rule around them changes. At present people leave a car on a charger overnight. From the first, a charging bay is for three hours, and after that it is an ordinary space and you may be asked to move.

One more thing, and it is the one that will cause the most argument. The old numbered spaces near the lift were the ones everyone wanted, and under the new system nobody owns them. They will go to whoever arrives first. I know that is not popular with the people who have had them for years, but the alternative is keeping a system where a third of the tarmac sits empty and our visitors park on the street.

narratorIntro: Now turn to Part two. You will hear a woman describing a summer activity programme for teenagers. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to twenty.
body: Hello, and thanks for coming along this evening. I run the summer programme at the sports centre, and this is the meeting where parents ask me the questions the leaflet doesn't answer.

The programme runs for six weeks. It starts on the eighth of July. It is for young people between twelve and sixteen. We take a maximum of sixty a week. The first two weeks fill up. The last one stays quiet. So if you have any choice, book late rather than early.

The day starts at nine and finishes at four. We supervise from half past eight and until half past four. There is no extra charge for that. It is there because most of you work. Beyond those hours we cannot supervise. I would rather say that plainly now.

The activities split into three strands. Water sports are on Mondays and Wednesdays. They take place at the reservoir, not here. There is a coach at half past eight. It does not wait. Court sports are Tuesdays and Thursdays and are here in the main hall. Fridays are the trip day, and the destination changes each week.

About cost. The week costs ninety-five pounds. That includes everything except the Friday trip. A trip costs between ten and twenty-five pounds. It depends where we go. You pay for it on the Monday of the same week. If a trip is cancelled for weather, you are refunded in full.

Lunch is not provided. There is a canteen and it is reasonable, but many young people bring their own, and there is a fridge they may use. We ask that nothing containing nuts comes into the building at all.

Now the question everybody asks. Yes, they can leave at lunchtime if you have signed the form. No, we cannot let them go without it. A phone call from you on the day is not enough. The form has to be signed once, at the start, and it lasts the whole summer.

Bookings open on the fourteenth of May at nine in the morning, online only. We do not take bookings by phone, and I am afraid we cannot hold a place for anyone, including for the families who came last year.

narratorIntro: Now turn to Part two. You will hear a man briefing new staff at a hotel on their first morning. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to twenty.
body: Good morning. I'm the duty manager, and this is the half hour where I tell you the things that are not in the handbook, or that are in it and get missed.

Start with your shifts. Early is seven until three, late is three until eleven, and you will be on a rota that changes every fortnight. The rota goes up on the Thursday before it starts. If you need a day, ask before the Thursday, because after it goes up I can only swap you with somebody who agrees.

Uniform. Shirts and aprons are provided and laundered here. Shoes are yours, and they must be closed at the toe. That is a kitchen rule that we apply everywhere, because everyone crosses the kitchen at some point.

Breaks. On an eight-hour shift you get one hour, and it is paid. Take it in the staff room on the second floor, not in the guest areas, and not at the back door, which is where people used to go and where guests can see you.

Now, the two rules I will not bend. The first is the key cards. Yours opens the rooms on your floor and the store cupboards. It does not open the office or the cellar, and if you find that it does, tell me, because that is a mistake and not a promotion. The second is the fire doors. They are held open by magnets and they close when the alarm sounds. Do not prop them, ever, not even for two minutes while you move a trolley.

About guests, one piece of advice rather than a rule. If a guest asks you something you do not know, do not guess. Say you will find out and then actually find out. Nearly every complaint I deal with started as a small wrong answer given confidently.

Finally, pay and problems. Pay goes in on the twenty-eighth, or the Friday before if that falls at a weekend. If something is wrong with it, come to me the same day, because the payroll cut-off is the third of the month and after that a correction waits until the next run.

— It is, and say it early rather than in a footnote. Now, what did you find?

— Careful. Used the most in total, or the most per person?

— If it doesn't survive, do we still report it?
— You report both. The raw figure and the per-person one, and you say which you think is the right unit and why. What you must not do is report only the one that makes the better story.
— Fine. Then the second finding is about the shower timers. We handed out fifty and got thirty-one back with the diaries filled in.
— That's a good return.
— The average shower fell from nine minutes to six in the first week. But by week four it was back to eight.
— That pattern is more interesting than the first-week figure, and it is the one people leave out. Why do you think it drifts back?
— We asked. The most common answer was that they stopped looking at it.
— Then say that, and say how you know. Now, timing. Your draft is due on the nineteenth?
— The twenty-second.
— Even better. Get the per-person recalculation done first, because if the first finding does not survive it, your whole introduction changes and there is no point polishing it before then.
— One last thing. Should we put the diaries in an appendix?
— Put a sample in, not all thirty-one. Three or four that show the range, and say how you chose them.
— Chose them how?
— However you like, as long as you say it. A reader can forgive a small sample and cannot forgive not knowing how it was picked.

narratorIntro: Now turn to Part three. You will hear a student, Ines, talking to her tutor about a reading list. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to thirty.
body: — So, the reading list. You said it was too long.
— It's forty items for eight weeks. Nobody reads forty items.
— Nobody is meant to. Did you notice it is in three sections?
— I saw the headings, but I assumed they were topics.
— They are not. The first eight are essential, the next twelve are recommended, and the rest is there if you write on that topic.
— That is not obvious from the document.
— No, and that is fair criticism. I will put a sentence at the top before next year. What made you read it as one list?
— The numbering. It runs from one to forty straight through, so it looks like a single sequence.
— That is a good point and an easy fix.
— Can I ask about the two book chapters in the essential eight? The library has one copy of each.
— Both are scanned. They are in the module folder, not the library catalogue, which is probably why you didn't find them.
— I looked in the catalogue for an hour.
— Then that is the second thing I need to fix. Now, about the essay. You are choosing between the migration topic and the housing one?
— Housing, I think. There's more written on it.
— There is more written on it, which cuts both ways. It is easier to find sources and harder to say anything that has not been said.
— Would you steer us away from it?
— No. I would steer you towards a narrower version of it. Housing in general has been done. Housing policy in one city over one decade has not, and it is the same amount of reading.
— That sounds more manageable, actually.

— It usually is. One more thing: the word limit is two thousand, and the penalty above it is steep — five per cent for every hundred words. People lose a grade to that every year, almost always because they left the editing until the last evening.
— Can we use sources that aren't on the list at all?
— Please do. The list is a floor, not a ceiling, and the best essays every year use something I have not read.
— How many extra would you expect?
— I would not put a number on it. Two well-chosen ones are worth ten that are there to lengthen the bibliography, and a marker can tell the difference within a paragraph.
— That's useful. Thank you.

narratorIntro: Now turn to Part three. You will hear a student, Danny, discussing a work placement with his course tutor. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to thirty.
body: — Sit down. You wanted to talk about the placement.
— Yes. I've had two offers and I can't decide.
— Tell me about them.
— The first is a small architecture practice, six people, in the city centre. The second is a large engineering consultancy in Bristol, employing about four hundred professional staff.
— And the work?
— At the small practice I'd be doing a bit of everything. Drawings, site visits, some client meetings. At the large firm I'd be in one team, working on drainage.
— Which one are you leaning towards?
— The small one, because it sounds more interesting. But everyone tells me the big name looks better afterwards.
— Let me push back on that. Whose name is on your degree certificate?
— The university's.
— And who reads your placement report?
— My supervisor here.

— So the name matters less than you have been told. What matters considerably more is what you can describe in an interview, and somebody who has attempted five different activities explains them more convincingly than somebody who has perfected one.
— That's an odd way to put it.

— It is, and it is not quite what I mean. I mean that breadth gives you more to say. But there is a serious argument on the other side, and you should hear it properly. Drainage is unglamorous, and it is simultaneously where the money is, so a summer of specialisation makes you employable in a way that a summer of variety does not.
— So you are saying both.
— I am saying the question is not which is better. It is which one you would still be glad of in two years. Now, some practical things. Are they both paid?
— The large firm pays. The small one offers expenses only.
— Then that is a substantial difference, and you should not pretend otherwise. How far away is Bristol for you?
— An hour and a half each way.
— Three hours a day. Add that up over ten weeks before you decide.
— I hadn't.
— Most people haven't. One last thing: the placement report is due two weeks after you finish, not at the start of term. People miss that every year.
— Should I tell the one I turn down straight away?
— Yes, and this week. They will have a second choice waiting and it is a small profession. A late refusal is remembered longer than a quick one.
— And do I say why?
— A sentence is plenty. You do not owe anybody a paragraph, and a long explanation usually reads as an apology for a decision that needed none.

narratorIntro: Now turn to Part three. You will hear a student, Priya, planning a presentation with her tutor. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to thirty.
body: — How far have you got with the presentation?
— We have collected the material. My partner and I cannot agree about the structure.
— Go on.

— I want to start with the case study and draw the theory out of it, but my partner wants the theory first. My anxiety is that beginning with a single institution will persuade the audience that the entire presentation concerns that institution.

— That is a genuine risk, and there is a compromise available. Open with two minutes of the case study, pause deliberately, identify the questions it raises, and then move to the theoretical material. You keep the attention and you keep the framing.
— That would work. How long have we got?
— Fifteen minutes and five for questions, and the fifteen is enforced. I stop people at fifteen.
— Even mid-sentence?
— Especially mid-sentence. It is the only way it stays fair.
— How many slides is sensible?

— That is the wrong question entirely. The better question concerns how many ideas, and the answer is approximately four. Some presenters use twenty slides for four ideas and others use precisely four, and either approach can succeed.
— We had thirty-one.
— Then you have more than four ideas, or you have four ideas and a lot of decoration.
— Mostly graphs.

— Graphs are the commonest decoration of all. Interrogate each one about whether the audience can genuinely read it during the six seconds it remains visible. Otherwise it belongs in a handout rather than a presentation.
— Should we hand anything out?
— One page, afterwards, never before. Before, and they read it instead of listening.
— And who speaks when?

— That remains your decision, although you should not alternate at every slide. Two extended turns outperform eight abbreviated ones, because every handover costs the audience approximately ten seconds of concentration.
— What about the questions? Neither of us is confident there.

— Agree in advance who takes what. If a question arrives that neither of you can answer, say so and offer to follow up. The worst answer in a presentation is a confident invention, and the panel always knows.
— Do you want us to rehearse it in front of you?
— I would rather you rehearsed it in front of somebody who does not know the subject. I will nod along at things that are not clear, because I already know what you mean.
— That is a fair point.
— Find a flatmate, and ask them afterwards what the four ideas were. If they can only name two, you have your answer about the slides.

narratorIntro: Now turn to Part four. You will hear part of a lecture on the history of standardised time. First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
body: I want to begin with an observation that sounds trivial and turns out to organise the whole subject. Before the middle of the nineteenth century, almost every town in Britain kept its own time, and the difference between them was not an inconvenience because nothing travelled faster than a horse. Bristol was approximately ten minutes behind London, Oxford five, and nobody was troubled by this, because the two clocks were never in the same room.

What destroyed local time was not a philosophical argument about measurement. It was the railway timetable. A train leaving London at nine and arriving in Bristol at eleven arrives, in local reckoning, at ten to eleven, and if the return service is scheduled on Bristol time the two are irreconcilable. The companies solved this unilaterally: the Great Western adopted London time throughout its network in 1840, and the other companies followed within a decade. Notice the sequence, because it recurs throughout the history of standardisation. A private operator imposes a convention for its own convenience; the public adopts it because the alternative is confusion; and the state ratifies it long afterwards, in this case in 1880, when Parliament finally defined legal time.

The international version of this story is usually told as the Washington conference of 1884, at which the prime meridian was fixed at Greenwich. That telling is misleading in one respect worth correcting. The conference did not choose Greenwich because Britain argued persuasively. It chose Greenwich because something like seventy per cent of the world's shipping already used charts based on it, and the delegates were ratifying a fact rather than making a decision. France abstained, and continued to publish Paris-based longitude for a further twenty-seven years, which tells you how much a conference resolution weighs against an installed base.

Now, the aspect I find most interesting, and which is least often discussed. Standard time created a category that had not previously existed: the person who is late. When each town kept its own hour, lateness was a local and negotiable matter. Once a timetable is printed and a clock in the station is authoritative, lateness becomes a measurable failure attributable to an individual, and the vocabulary of industrial discipline follows almost immediately. The factory whistle, the clocking-in card and the docked quarter-hour all postdate the railway clock rather than preceding it.

I would not want to push that causal claim too hard. Punctuality as a virtue is older than the railway; you find it in monastic rules centuries earlier. What changed was not the value but its enforceability, and the enforcement required a shared and unarguable reference. That is the pattern I want you to take away. A standard does not merely describe a practice more precisely. It changes what can be demanded, and therefore who can be blamed.

For next week, read the Zerubavel chapter, which is short, and the Bartky article, which is not. Bartky is the one that goes through the American railway companies' negotiations in detail, and it is worth the effort because it shows the process working without a government in the room at all.

narratorIntro: Now turn to Part four. You will hear part of a lecture on the economics of seed banks. First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
body: Seed banks are usually presented to the public as insurance, and the analogy is instructive precisely where it breaks down. Insurance pays out in money, which is fungible; a seed bank pays out in biological material that must still be viable, still be identified correctly, and still be adapted to a climate that has moved since the sample was taken. Each of those three conditions fails at a different rate, and the interesting economics lie in the differences.

Viability first. Most orthodox seeds — that is, seeds that tolerate drying and freezing — retain germination capacity for decades at minus twenty degrees, and the standard practice is to test a subsample every ten years and to regenerate the accession when germination falls below eighty-five per cent. Regeneration means growing the plants out and harvesting fresh seed, and it is by a considerable margin the largest recurring cost a bank carries. For a collection of forty thousand accessions, regeneration is not an occasional event; it is the permanent condition of the institution.

The identification problem is less obvious and, in my view, more serious. A seed is only as useful as its passport data — where it was collected, from what population, under what conditions. Roughly a fifth of the material in older collections has passport data that is incomplete or demonstrably wrong, usually because it was copied by hand across three or four transfers between institutions. A sample without reliable provenance is not worthless, but it is worth dramatically less, because a breeder cannot tell whether the drought tolerance they observe is genetic or an artefact of where it was grown.

The third condition is the one that undermines the insurance framing altogether. A wheat landrace collected in Anatolia in 1955 was adapted to the Anatolia of 1955. Restoring it in 2060 does not restore its fitness, because the environment it was fitted to no longer exists in that form. What the bank actually preserves is not a solution but a set of genetic options, and options have value only if somebody has the capacity to use them. That capacity — the breeding programmes, the field trials, the people — is funded on three-year cycles, while the seeds are stored on a fifty-year horizon. The mismatch between those two timescales is the central problem of the field, and it is a problem of institutions rather than of biology.

Which brings me to duplication. Every major collection is supposed to hold a safety duplicate elsewhere, and about two thirds do. The remaining third is usually described as a funding gap, and it is partly that, but it is also a coordination failure: duplication benefits everyone and is paid for by one party, which is the classic structure of a good that gets underprovided.

For the seminar, read the Fowler piece and come with a position on whether the Svalbard model — free deposit, depositor retains ownership — is the right one, or whether it makes the coordination problem worse by removing the pressure to negotiate.

narratorIntro: Now turn to Part four. You will hear part of a lecture on the acoustics of concert halls. First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
body: The history of concert hall acoustics is a history of a single number being taken too seriously, and then not seriously enough. The number is reverberation time, defined by Wallace Sabine in the eighteen nineties as the interval required for sound to decay by sixty decibels, and Sabine's formula, which relates it to the volume of the room divided by its total absorption, is still the first thing anyone calculates.

For about sixty years, reverberation time was treated as very nearly the whole subject. Halls were designed to a target — around two seconds for orchestral music, rather less for opera, less again for speech — and if the number came out right the hall was expected to sound right. The Royal Festival Hall, opened in 1951, is the instructive failure. Its reverberation time was almost exactly as specified. Musicians disliked it immediately, audiences found it dry, and the disagreement between the measurement and the perception took a generation to explain.

The explanation, when it arrived, concerned the early reflections: the sound that reaches a listener within roughly the first eighty milliseconds after the direct sound. Those early arrivals are not heard as echo. They are fused with the direct sound and perceived as loudness and as intimacy, and their lateral component in particular — sound arriving from the sides rather than from above — produces the sense of being enveloped that musicians describe and that no single decay figure captures. This is why the narrow rectangular halls of the nineteenth century, built before anyone could calculate anything, outperform many of the fan-shaped halls designed afterwards with far better instruments. A narrow room delivers strong lateral reflections from close side walls as a matter of geometry. A wide fan-shaped room delivers the first reflections from the ceiling, and they arrive from the wrong direction.

There is a second reason the older halls do well, and it is unfashionable to mention because it is not acoustic. They are small. The Musikverein seats around eighteen hundred and the Concertgebouw about two thousand, where a modern hall is asked to seat between two and three thousand to be financially viable. Every additional seat moves somebody further from the stage, and there is no arrangement of surfaces that compensates for distance.

What modern practice does, and does well, is measure more things: clarity, lateral energy fraction, strength, the ratio of early to late energy. What it cannot do is escape the constraint that the client's brief and the acoustician's brief are in tension. The former asks for seats; the latter asks for proximity and for side walls close enough to be useful. Where a modern hall succeeds, it has usually succeeded by winning that argument in the first month of the project rather than by clever surface treatment in the last.

Read the Beranek survey for next week. His rankings are contestable and he says so, but the value is in the correlations he reports between the subjective judgements of musicians and the measurable quantities, and in how weak some of them are.

narratorIntro: Now turn to Part four. You will hear part of a lecture on the archaeology of roads. First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
body: Roads are the most abundant archaeological feature in Europe and among the least excavated, and the reason is a practical one that tells you something about the discipline. A road is linear, which means that to sample it representatively you would have to trench it at intervals over tens of kilometres, and funding is awarded for sites rather than for lines. Almost everything we know about Roman road construction therefore comes from a small number of sections cut where a modern road or pipeline happened to cross an old one, which is to say from a sample selected by the twentieth century rather than by us.

With that caveat in place, the standard account runs as follows. A major Roman road was built in layers: a levelled and compacted foundation, a bedding of larger stone, a layer of smaller graded material, and a surface, sometimes of fitted slabs but far more often of compacted gravel. The slabbed roads of the tourist photograph are urban and are a small minority of the network. What matters structurally is drainage. The road was raised on an agger, a bank of material, with ditches on both sides, and where those ditches were maintained the road survived and where they were not it did not, regardless of how well the layers had been laid.

Now the interpretive question I want to spend the rest of the hour on. It is usually said that the Romans built straight roads. They did, over much of the distance, and the explanation normally offered is military efficiency: a straight road is the shortest and moves troops fastest. That explanation is weaker than it looks. The roads deviate constantly at the local scale, following contours and avoiding wet ground, and a survey of the Fosse Way found that the longest genuinely straight segment is about eleven kilometres, not the hundreds of the popular imagination. Straightness is an artefact of the surveying method — sighting between high points — rather than a doctrine about lines.

What is more interesting is what the roads avoid. They avoid existing settlements far more often than they connect them, which is inconvenient for the model in which roads follow trade. They connect forts, and they connect forts to ports. The commercial network appears afterwards, growing along an infrastructure built for another purpose, and the towns that prosper are the ones that happen to sit where the military network already ran. If you want a single generalisation to take from this lecture, that is the one: the infrastructure precedes the economy that later appears to explain it, and reading the map backwards from the towns produces a confident and wrong account of why the roads are where they are.

For next week, look at the Davies chapter on the surveying instruments, and if you have time the Bishop article on the agger. Bishop is the one who argues that the drainage, not the paving, is the technology, and I want to hear whether you find that persuasive.
